newsitem.title: EU: EU casts doubts on British plan to ease beef ban.
newsitem.headline: EU casts doubts on British plan to ease beef ban.

text.p: The European Commission has cast doubt on a British proposal for easing a ban on British exports of beef imposed because of fears over mad cow disease, an aide to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Friday.
The doubts were expressed in a joint letter from Fischler and EU food safety commissioner Emma Bonino, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

The letter is another blow for the ruling Conservative government, widely blamed for mishandling the crisis over Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and looks set to maintain tensions with the EU before Britain's May 1 election.

Britain, urgently trying to persuade the EU to ease the economically and politically harmful ban, in February proposed setting up a "certified herd scheme" to identify cows from BSE-free herds which could then be exported.
"The scheme looks very complex and in the absence of computerised records it's hard to see how it would work," the aide told Reuters.
The complexity is due to the definition of two categories of beef -- whether or not it contains bone -- and the period in which herds have been free from disease.
They also said a new British central computerised system to keep track of healthy cows had been set up too recently to be of any use at this stage.
In 1988, Northern Ireland introduced a computerised system for recording all cattle movements from birth to slaughter and data on BSE and other animal illnesses.
In the rest of Britain a compulsory cattle passport system was only introduced in July, 1996, and was followed by computerised data bases.

"We feel that the management of this system will be relatively simple in Northern Ireland with with its well-established computerised database and terminals in the abattoirs," the commissioners said in the letter to British farm minister Douglas Hogg.

"However, in Great Britain the certification of these animals will depend on the declarations made by the farmer and it is hard to see how the relevant information can be given by the keeper of an animal for all movements prior to the time at which he acquired it," they added.

The commissioners said they were also concerned that British vets seemed to be against the certified herd scheme, adding: "Unless the veterinarians are willing to sign the necessary certificates, it will be impossible to make progress on the issue."
On Tuesday Bonino's spokesman Filippo di Robilant said EU scientists had been asked to report by the end of May on the British proposal to exempt certified BSE-free herds.
Euroopean Commission spokesmen have ruled out any early easing of the EU ban, imposed in March last year after Britain linked BSE to a fatal human illness, Creutzfeldt-Jakob-Disease (CJD).

Hogg said on Friday Britain had complied fully with an agreement signed in Florence last June providing a framework for a lifting of the ban, and accused EU countries of dragging their feet for domestic reasons.

He denied the letter represented bad news, saying the commissioners agreed there would be no problems using the new scheme in Northern Ireland and for home-bred animals, as well as those from herds which had not been moved around too much.

"In other words, in respect of a quite a wide number of our herds and cattle the scheme is a good one and the commissioners accept that," he told BBC radio, taking the opportunity to launch another sideswipe at Britain's European partners.
"What (this) does prove is the reluctance of the European agriculture ministers, responding to their own domestic pressure from farmers and consumers, to make a move," he said.
The opposition Labour party, which has a big opinion poll lead over the Conservatives, has consistently attacked the government and Hogg in particular over the BSE crisis.
On Tuesday, Major called for an end to the ban and hinted he would sack Hogg if he won the election.
